    <id>http://arxiv.org/abs/2611.26398v1</id>
    <title>Democratizing Cross-Project Knowledge for Transforming Water Governance and Climate Resilience: an Agentic AI Ecosystem</title>
    <updated>2026-11-19T16:49:04Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.26398v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.26398v1" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>EU-funded projects produce extensive evidence in the form of deliverables, reports, and case studies. However, this knowledge is typically scattered across projects and document structures, making it difficult to locate relevant, contextual information when making decisions. This paper introduces an Agentic AI Ecosystem that consolidates heterogeneous project documentation into a domain-aware knowledge base and provides adaptive access through an agentic Retrieval-Augmented Generation pipeline. Documents from three EU-funded projects (IMPETUS, NATALIE, and InnWater) are reconstructed into hierarchical section trees and indexed with structured metadata. Retrieval is supported by two domain-specific embedding models fine-tuned on domain data (water and climate). On top of this knowledge base, a ReAct-style controller iteratively orchestrates retrieval actions by allocating retrieval budget across domain collections and accumulating evidence until a stopping criterion is met. In a retrieval benchmark over the corpus, the proposed approach improves Mean Reciprocal Rank by 26.7% (relative) compared to a single-domain embedding baseline, indicating more consistent retrieval of relevant evidence to support cross-project knowledge synthesis and climate-resilient decision-making.</summary>

    <id>http://arxiv.org/abs/2611.10405v1</id>
    <title>Yuanbao-Reranker: Document-Grounded Synthesis and Preference Distillation for Text Reranking</title>
    <updated>2026-11-07T02:30:44Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.10405v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.10405v1" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>High-precision text reranking is a critical component in modern search, recommendation, and agentic retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) systems. We present Yuanbao-Reranker, a family of general-purpose dense rerankers spanning 0.6B, 4B, and 8B parameter scales built upon the Qwen3 backbone. To construct diverse and reliable ranking supervision at scale, we pair answer-first and query-type-guided document-grounded synthesis with a three-stage curation funnel that verifies positive support, eliminates semantic redundancy, and enforces balanced source-by-length quotas. For each curated pair, we screen real retrieval pools with a teacher score margin to filter out potential false negatives and sample Hard, Medium, and Moderate negative tiers, yielding 2.75M $1{:}3$ ranking groups. We train the models by jointly optimizing pointwise relevance cross-entropy and a bounded minimum-gap hinge objective over both positive--negative and negative--negative pairs. This formulation transfers fine-grained teacher preferences across candidate tiers without over-constraining well-separated predictions, supporting both cross-scale and same-scale distillation followed by layerwise adaptive model merging. Across five comprehensive benchmarks spanning Chinese (CMTEB-R), multilingual (MMTEB-R), English (BEIR), long-document (MLDR), and code (MTEB-Code) retrieval, Yuanbao-Reranker consistently leads every parameter tier: the 0.6B variant reaches 70.96 Avg. to surpass 1B--4B active-parameter baselines, the 4B variant reaches 73.63 Avg. to outperform the 8B teacher (72.68), and the 8B variant achieves a state-of-the-art 74.21 Avg., with substantial gains generalizing across distinct first-stage retrievers.</summary>

    <id>http://arxiv.org/abs/2610.36444v1</id>
    <title>RouteDRAG: Learning to Route and Control Agentic Execution for Multimodal Document RAG</title>
    <updated>2026-10-27T00:45:49Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.36444v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.36444v1" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>Web-based applications increasingly rely on understanding long multimodal documents, where answering questions often requires combining information across pages, tables, and figures. Agentic retrieval-augmented generation addresses these tasks through iterative retrieval and reasoning. However, Agentic execution is not always necessary, introducing additional computation and potentially incorrect answers. Our empirical analysis reveals that Agentic execution provides query-dependent benefits, while additional operations may improve, preserve, or degrade answer accuracy. These findings motivate controlling both Agent invocation and subsequent execution. To address these challenges, we propose RouteDRAG, a learning-based framework comprising four components. Unified Document Index organizes multimodal content into a graph-backed index and derives query representations from initial retrieval. Adaptive Path Routing preserves exact answering and predicts the relative benefit of Agent over shorter execution paths. Dynamic Agent Execution maintains an evolving workspace and refines Planner proposals to control tool use and termination. Sequential Policy Learning first trains operation control from observed outcomes and then trains path routing using the resulting Agent's performance. Across two benchmarks, RouteDRAG achieves an average accuracy improvement of 3.47 percentage points over shorter-path-only execution while assigning only 79.3% of queries to Agent. Notably, it also surpasses uniform Agent execution on both benchmarks while requiring fewer answering calls. Our code is now available at https://github.com/Ereshkigal1/RouteDRAG.</summary>

    <id>http://arxiv.org/abs/2610.35240v1</id>
    <title>Reading Beyond OCR Noise: Robust Cross-Lingual RAG for Legislative Archives</title>
    <updated>2026-10-26T11:24:16Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.35240v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.35240v1" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>India's historical public archives present severe computer vision and document image analysis challenges: decades of parliamentary records survive only as degraded, multi-column scanned pages featuring mixed scripts, complex layouts, and dense visual noise where OCR failure is the primary obstacle to information retrieval. We present an end-to-end framework that couples vision-based layout segmentation and multi-script OCR with an agentic retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) pipeline. Our approach specifically addresses how visual degradation and layout fragmentation propagate into text extraction errors, using an iterative agentic loop to navigate around OCR noise and layout ambiguities before generating answers. Evaluated on the 200,000-page Punjab Vidhan Sabha archive, our system demonstrates robust handling of historical document degradation, outperforming standard text-only baselines.</summary>

    <id>http://arxiv.org/abs/2610.25096v3</id>
    <title>Toward Agentic Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Enterprise Retail Workflows over Heterogeneous Data Sources</title>
    <updated>2026-11-18T14:56:15Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.25096v3" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.25096v3" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>Enterprise retail workflows require agents to chain evidence across heterogeneous sources, from structured product and order records to unstructured inquiries and reviews, yet existing agentic RAG benchmarks rarely capture this challenge. To enable controlled evaluation of such workflows, we introduce RetailBridge, a compositional retail benchmark built from persona-driven simulations. Its questions are constructed by linking entities and intermediate answers across heterogeneous sources, requiring agents to identify the relevant sources, carry evidence between them, and produce a grounded answer. To systematically evaluate LLMs on these retail workflows, we develop RetailRAG, a retail-aware framework equipped with auto-schema briefing, source-routed plan chaining, and diagnostic plan revision. RetailRAG consistently outperforms existing agentic RAG baselines across all evaluation axes, serving as a strong reference system for assessing LLM agents on retail workflows. On RetailBridge, evaluating ten LLM backbones with RetailRAG reveals multi-source chaining as the dominant bottleneck across providers and model scales, suggesting that reliable retail agents require explicit cross-source orchestration rather than scaling alone. Code and data are publicly available at https://github.com/DISL-Lab/RetailBridge.</summary>

    <id>http://arxiv.org/abs/2610.11899v1</id>
    <title>Forms of LLM-Integrated Applications from LLM-Chats to Autonomous AI Agent System</title>
    <updated>2026-10-08T13:05:33Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.11899v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.11899v1" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly embedded as components in software systems, marketed under labels such as chatbot, copilot, retrieval-augmented generation, workflow, coding agent and AI agent. Whether these labels denote genuine architectural forms or serve as branding has not been assessed systematically.
  In the sources surveyed, labels do carry architectural content, most clearly in vendor usage: copilot denotes a router-worker architecture operating a host application under step-by-step user confirmation, while the more recent shift to the label agent coincides with AI-planned multi-step execution of which the user sees only the outcome. The coding agents of four major providers share one architecture, a reason-and-act loop delegating to subagents.
  This survey describes seven recurring forms---LLM chats, custom agents, retrieval-augmented generation (RAG), AI-enhanced workflows, copilots, coding agents, and, in part, agentic RAG---in a common vocabulary of agents and tools. Each is characterized along four structural dimensions (agentic RAG only partially): the architectural pattern, the control of execution and the point of user intervention, the number of agent calls per task, and tool use. An illustrative corpus of 22 systems from research publications and vendor documentation grounds the descriptions and shows where they reach their limit.</summary>

    <id>http://arxiv.org/abs/2610.05034v1</id>
    <title>Agentic RAG Evaluation: Budget Allocation Across Questions, Trajectories, and Reads</title>
    <updated>2026-10-04T07:55:34Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.05034v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.05034v1" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>Evaluation budgets in agentic retrieval-augmented generation span questions, search trajectories, and repeated answers. We measure allocation precision, reading efficiency, and cost boundaries using a retrieval-feedback comparison on HotpotQA and MuSiQue. At 34.14--34.39M model tokens, broader question coverage lowers standard error by 33\% versus five reads and 12.6\% versus three trajectories. Archived nested and Q-only forecasts predict these allocations within 4.0\% and 3.5\%, respectively. Depth subsets establish no clear forecasting advantage beyond the two-trajectory audit. One-read variance penalties relative to the fitted optimum at the same token budget are 0--9.9\%, with substantial Pro uncertainty. Under recorded model fees, more questions beat more trajectories at search prices of \$0--1 per 1,000 requests; question-versus-read fee rankings remain unresolved. Temperature zero cuts answer disagreement from 14.3\% to 3.4\% while comparison precision stays similar. \par\medskip\noindent\textbf{Keywords:} Agentic RAG; Evaluation budget; Generalizability theory; Repeated sampling.</summary>

    <id>http://arxiv.org/abs/2609.35215v1</id>
    <title>ASCT: Attentive Search over Counterfactual Trees for Credit Assignment in Agentic Reinforcement Learning</title>
    <updated>2026-09-28T14:04:20Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.35215v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2609.35215v1" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>Terminal utility evaluates a complete agentic workflow, but learning requires credit for the decisions within it. We introduce Attentive Search over Counterfactual Trees (ASCT), a framework that turns training-time multi-step search into local action credit. At actor-visited states, an auxiliary tree evaluates alternative legal actions from the same recoverable prefix. Its action-value table is centered by the frozen actor's probabilities and supplies credit for PPO on actor-sampled trajectories. This protocol connects counterfactual evaluation to policy learning while deploying the actor alone. Uniform, UCT, and cost-aware AgentUCT instantiate the framework. On HotpotQA agentic retrieval-augmented generation, all three improve mean held-out utility over trajectory-return PPO and workflow-adapted VinePPO. Across three seeds, ASCT-AgentUCT reaches 0.6187 utility versus 0.5939 for VinePPO, with gains in answer F1 and execution cost, and uses 50.3% fewer recorded auxiliary Qwen tokens. Transfer and component-description studies examine the learned policies beyond the training setting.</summary>

    <id>http://arxiv.org/abs/2609.37468v1</id>
    <title>Backdoor in the Loop: Compromising Agentic Search via Malicious Retrievers</title>
    <updated>2026-09-26T14:47:25Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.37468v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2609.37468v1" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>Agentic retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) interleaves reasoning with repeated retrieval, giving the retriever influence over both the evidence an agent observes and its subsequent search decisions. We study retriever backdoors that exploit this feedback loop and repurpose weak backdoor purification to conceal their presence. An attacker supplies a compromised retriever checkpoint while leaving the search agent and deployment corpus unchanged. Without corpus write access, the attacker can still suppress useful evidence, persistently retrieve a selected existing document, or steer the agent toward prolonged search, inflating retrieval, context, and latency cost. To conceal these behaviors from detection, we propose leveraging a controlled inject-and-remove cycle: deliberately inject a weaker backdoor and then unlearn it. This process weakens detector-visible signatures and fools the backdoor detectors with an illusion of purification while preserving the malicious retrieval behavior. These findings expose a systematic vulnerability in RAG systems in which a weak defense becomes an attacker's concealment tool for a backdoored retriever, even when the underlying corpus remains trustworthy.</summary>

    <id>http://arxiv.org/abs/2609.23056v2</id>
    <title>Bridging Static and Agentic RAG for Taiwanese Historical Question Answering</title>
    <updated>2026-11-01T04:40:47Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.23056v2" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2609.23056v2" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>Agentic retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) enables language models to adapt retrieval based on previously retrieved evidence, but it remains unclear whether such adaptive orchestration consistently outperforms well-designed static pipelines. We conduct a controlled comparison of agentic and static RAG for Taiwanese historical question answering, sharing the same generator and hybrid retrieval backend. Despite similar aggregate performance, the two pipelines differ on 70.83% of questions, with their advantages largely canceling out when averaged. An oracle that selects the better response per question improves the composite score by 0.2417 over the better individual pipeline, revealing substantial headroom for question-level selection. We therefore introduce a post-hoc selector that compares the two responses and their cited evidence, significantly outperforming either individual pipeline and recovering 60.34% of the oracle headroom. These results show that aggregate comparisons can obscure meaningful question-level differences between retrieval strategies, suggesting that exploiting their complementarity may be more fruitful than seeking a universally superior pipeline.</summary>
